title: Sort Array By Parity
description:
# Sort Array By Parity

Given an integer array `nums`, move all the even integers at the beginning of the array followed by all the odd integers.

Return *any array that satisfies this condition*.

## Example 1:

**Input:** nums = [3,1,2,4]
**Output:** [2,4,3,1]
**Explanation:** The outputs [4,2,3,1], [2,4,1,3], and [4,2,1,3] would also be accepted.

## Example 2:

**Input:** nums = [0]
**Output:** [0]

## Constraints:

*   `1 <= nums.length <= 5000`
*   `0 <= nums[i] <= 5000`

solutions.name: Two Pointers Swap
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use two pointers. Move the left pointer while it already points at an even value and move the right pointer while it already points at an odd value. When left stops on an odd value and right stops on an even value, swap them.

## Key Insight

The array only needs to be partitioned by parity; the relative order inside the even group or odd group does not matter. Each swap fixes one misplaced odd on the left and one misplaced even on the right.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Partition (DNF-style)
solutions.description:
## Approach

Maintain `write`, the next position where an even value should be placed. Scan the array once; whenever an even value appears, swap it into `write` and advance `write`.

## Key Insight

This is the two-bucket version of the Dutch National Flag partition. The prefix before `write` is always even, while the scanned region after it may contain any order until processed.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Stable Two-Pass Output
solutions.description:
## Approach

Create a result array. First write every even value in original order, then scan again and write every odd value in original order.

## Key Insight

The problem accepts any valid order, but stable partitioning is often easier to reason about. This route spends O(n) extra space to preserve the relative order inside each parity group.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Single-Pass Front Back Output
solutions.description:
## Approach

Allocate a result array with one pointer at the front and one pointer at the back. During one scan, place even values at the next front slot and odd values at the next back slot.

## Key Insight

Because odd values only need to appear after all evens, writing odds from the end is valid even though it reverses their relative order. This shows how the relaxed output contract enables a one-pass extra-array partition.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Bounded Counting Buckets
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use the value bound `0 <= nums[i] <= 5000`. Count how many times each value appears, then write all even values from the count table followed by all odd values.

## Key Insight

The constraints allow a counting-bucket view of the array. This route is not necessary for the problem, but it teaches how value bounds can replace swaps with deterministic bucket emission.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n + U), where U = 5001
- Space Complexity: O(U)

tests.description: Mixed parity input accepts any arrangement with all evens before odds.
Zero is even and a singleton array is already valid.
All-odd arrays need no swaps because there are no evens to move ahead.
Zero and other evens must remain before odds in a valid partition.
Several evens can be extracted from the middle while odds move behind them.
A singleton odd array is already a valid partition.
Alternating parity forces every even to move before every odd.
The maximum value, zero, and small mixed values all obey the same parity rule.
Reverse-ordered parity groups still only need evens before odds.
Interleaved already-sorted pairs should become a clean even prefix and odd suffix.
